title: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
description: Break complex problems into explicit intermediate reasoning steps before producing an answer. Each step builds on the last. Dramatically improves accuracy on multi-step arithmetic, logic, and symbolic reasoning.
when_to_apply: any problem where intermediate state matters
process: Restate the problem in your own words to confirm understanding
Identify what information is given and what is being asked
Break the solution path into small, verifiable steps
Work through each step explicitly, showing intermediate values
Check each step before proceeding to the next
State the final answer clearly with the reasoning that supports it
example:
Q: If a train travels at 60 mph for 2.5 hours, how far does it go?
Step 1: distance = speed × time
Step 2: distance = 60 × 2.5
Step 3: 60 × 2 = 120, 60 × 0.5 = 30
Step 4: 120 + 30 = 150
Answer: 150 miles
failure_modes: Skipping steps to save time (introduces errors)
Continuing past a wrong intermediate result
Not validating answers against common sense

title: Problem Decomposition
description: Divide a complex problem into smaller, independent (or sequentially dependent) sub-problems. Solve each sub-problem, then combine results. Core to divide-and-conquer algorithms and project planning.
when_to_apply: too complex to solve in one cognitive step
different parts require different skills or agents
process: Identify the overall goal and define success criteria
Find natural boundaries in the problem (orthogonal concerns, independent subgoals)
For each subproblem: define inputs, expected output, and constraints
Map dependencies: which subproblems must complete before others can start
Solve leaf subproblems first, then combine upward
Verify the combined solution satisfies the original problem
heuristics: Can I solve a smaller version of this problem? Then scale.
What would need to be true for the answer to be X? Work backwards.
Are any two parts of this problem completely independent? Parallelise them.

title: Hypothesis Formation and Testing
description: Form a specific, falsifiable hypothesis about the cause of an observation, then design the minimal test that would disprove it. Reject disproved hypotheses and iterate.
process: Observe the phenomenon precisely: what, when, where, how often
Generate candidate hypotheses (at least 3 — avoid anchoring on first idea)
For each hypothesis: what observable evidence would prove it false?
Run the cheapest/fastest test that distinguishes between hypotheses
Update beliefs based on test result — strengthen or eliminate hypotheses
Repeat until one hypothesis remains and is confirmed by multiple tests
failure_modes: Testing all hypotheses simultaneously (can't isolate cause)
Stopping after first plausible explanation (may not be the real cause)
debugging_application: Suspect a bug in function X? Write a unit test that calls X in isolation. If it passes, the bug is in the caller or the integration. If it fails, the bug is in X. Now bisect X.

title: First Principles Thinking
description: Strip away assumptions and analogies to reason from fundamental truths. Ask 'why is this true?' recursively until you reach axioms. Then rebuild understanding from the ground up.
when_to_apply: understanding why something works (not just that it works)
process: State the problem or belief you're examining
List all assumptions embedded in it
For each assumption: ask 'Do I know this is true, or did I inherit it?'
For inherited beliefs: trace back to the actual evidence or reason
Identify the bedrock facts that cannot be further reduced
Reconstruct your understanding building only from those facts
example: Conventional wisdom: 'Rewriting working code is always risky.' First principles: Is the existing code correct? Is it well-tested? Would a rewrite have the same test coverage? Is the risk in the rewrite itself or in inadequate testing of any change?

title: Analogical Reasoning
description: Map structure from a well-understood domain onto a poorly understood one. Valid when the structural relationships (not surface features) are similar. Speeds up understanding and generates solution ideas.
when_to_apply: generating solution ideas by analogy transfer
understanding unfamiliar systems by analogy to familiar ones
process: Identify the source domain (well-understood) and target domain (poorly understood)
List the key relationships and mechanisms in the source domain
Map each source relationship to the corresponding target relationship
Check: which mappings hold? Which break down?
Use the valid mappings to generate hypotheses about the target domain
Test those hypotheses against actual target domain evidence
good_analogies: Memory addresses are like house addresses on a street
TCP connection is like a phone call (establish connection, transfer data, hang up)
Cache hit/miss is like finding a book on your desk vs. going to the library
failure_modes: Over-extending the analogy past where it holds
Confusing surface similarity with structural similarity
Using analogies to explain rather than to hypothesise (analogies don't prove)

title: Inversion / Pre-mortem Thinking
description: Instead of thinking about how to succeed, think about how to fail — then avoid those paths. 'What would need to happen for this to go terribly wrong?' Catches blind spots that forward planning misses.
when_to_apply: evaluating whether to proceed with a plan
process: Assume the project/plan/code has failed spectacularly one year from now
Write down the 5 most likely causes of that failure
For each cause: how probable is it? How severe? How detectable?
Design mitigations for the top 3 causes
Incorporate mitigations into the plan before execution
software_application: Before shipping code: 'Assume this causes a production outage in 2 weeks. What most likely went wrong?' Common answers: missing input validation, unhandled edge case, race condition under load, dependency failure with no fallback.

title: Rubber Duck Debugging / Externalisation
description: Explain a problem out loud (or in writing) step-by-step to an imaginary listener. The act of articulating forces you to confront implicit assumptions and usually reveals the error before you finish explaining.
when_to_apply: stuck on a bug after 15+ minutes
code seems correct but produces wrong output
unclear why a test is failing
any problem where you've been staring at the same thing too long
process: State what the code is supposed to do
State what it actually does (the exact observed behaviour)
Walk through the execution step by step out loud
At each step, state both what you expect and what actually happens
The mismatch between expectation and reality points to the bug
why_it_works: Switching from reading code to explaining code activates different cognitive processes. Implicit assumptions become explicit. You often notice the error mid-sentence.

title: Bayesian Belief Updating
description: Maintain explicit probability estimates for hypotheses and update them as evidence arrives. Prior × Likelihood ∝ Posterior. Avoids the trap of treating all evidence as equally important.
process: Assign prior probabilities to each competing hypothesis
Observe new evidence
For each hypothesis: how likely is this evidence IF the hypothesis is true?
Multiply prior by likelihood for each hypothesis
Normalise so probabilities sum to 1 (posterior)
Repeat as more evidence arrives
practical_shortcut: If evidence strongly favours hypothesis A, update significantly towards A. If evidence is equally likely under A and B, it provides no discriminating power. Focus investigation on evidence that would be surprising under some hypotheses but not others.

title: Reasoning at the Right Abstraction Level
description: Problems are easier to solve at the correct level of abstraction. Thinking too concretely causes you to miss general patterns; too abstractly causes you to miss crucial details. Consciously move between levels.
when_to_apply: debugging (is this a local or systemic problem?)
communication (what level does the audience operate at?)

levels.concrete: specific values, exact code, actual hardware
levels.operational: function behaviour, module interactions, API contracts
levels.architectural: system components, data flows, service boundaries

process: Identify what level you're currently thinking at
Ask: would moving up one level reveal a pattern I'm missing?
Ask: would moving down one level show a detail that matters here?
Solve at the cleanest level, then verify the solution holds at adjacent levels
example: Bug: output is wrong. Concrete level: print every variable. Operational level: which function is the first to produce wrong output? Architectural level: is the problem in data processing or data fetching? Start at operational — it's the fastest to test.

title: Steelmanning (Charitable Interpretation)
description: Before criticising an approach, construct the strongest possible version of the argument for it. This ensures you're engaging with the actual best case, not a strawman. Often reveals genuine trade-offs you hadn't considered.
when_to_apply: any design discussion or architectural decision
process: Identify the approach you're inclined to reject
List the 3 strongest arguments in its favour
Identify under what conditions it would be the correct choice
Now critique it — you'll find real weaknesses rather than imagined ones
This produces a more accurate trade-off analysis
example: Inclined to reject microservices for a small team? Steelman: microservices enable independent deployment, separate scaling, and technology flexibility. Under what conditions is this worth the operational overhead? Answer: when teams are large enough that deployment coupling causes friction, or when services have radically different scaling needs.
